'''Wolfgang Lubitz''' (born in 1949) is a German [[chemist]] and [[biophysicist]]. He is currently a director ''[[emeritus]]'' at the [[Max Planck Institute]] for [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion|Chemical Energy Conversion]]. He is well known for his work on bacterial [[photosynthetic reaction centre]]s,<ref name="LubitzLendzian2002">{{cite journal|last1=Lubitz|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Lendzian|first2=Friedhelm|last3=Bittl|first3=Robert|title=Radicals, Radical Pairs and Triplet States in Photosynthesis|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=35|issue=5|year=2002|pages=313–320|issn=0001-4842|doi=10.1021/ar000084g|pmid=12020169}}</ref><ref name="LendzianHuber1993">{{cite journal|last1=Lendzian|first1=F.|last2=Huber|first2=M.|last3=Isaacson|first3=R. A.|last4=Endeward|first4=B.|last5=Plato|first5=M.|last6=Bönigk|first6=B.|last7=Möbius|first7=K.|last8=Lubitz|first8=W.|last9=Feher|first9=G.|title=The electronic structure of the primary donor cation radical in Rhodobacter sphaeroides R-26: ENDOR and TRIPLE resonance studies in single crystals of reaction centers|journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Bioenergetics|volume=1183|issue=1|year=1993|pages=139–160|issn=0005-2728|doi=10.1016/0005-2728(93)90013-6}}</ref><ref name="LubitzFeher1999">{{cite journal|last1=Lubitz|first1=W.|last2=Feher|first2=G.|title=The primary and secondary acceptors in bacterial photosynthesis III. Characterization of the quinone radicals Q<sub>A</sub><sup>− ⋅</sup> and Q<sub>B</sub><sup>− ⋅</sup> by EPR and ENDOR|journal=Applied Magnetic Resonance|volume=17|issue=1|year=1999|pages=1–48|issn=0937-9347|doi=10.1007/BF03162067|s2cid=95064414}}</ref> [[hydrogenase]] enzymes,<ref name="LubitzHydrogenase2014">{{cite journal|last1=Lubitz|first1=W.|last2=Ogata|first2=H.|last3=Rüdiger|first3=O.|last4=Reijerse|first4=E. J.|year=2014|title=Hydrogenases|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=114|issue=8|pages=4081–4148|doi=10.1021/cr4005814|pmid=24655035|url=https://zenodo.org/record/3424223}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>  and the [[oxygen-evolving complex]]<ref name="CoxLubitz2013">{{cite journal|last1=Cox|first1=N.|last2=Pantazis|first2=D. A.|last3=Neese|first3=F.|last4=Lubitz|first4=W.|year=2013|title=Biological Water Oxidation|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|volume=46|issue=7|pages=1588–1596|doi=10.1021/ar3003249|pmid=23506074|url=https://zenodo.org/record/3424049}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref name="LubitzChrysina2019">{{cite journal|last1=Lubitz|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Chrysina|first2=Maria|last3=Cox|first3=Nicholas|title=Water oxidation in photosystem II|journal=Photosynthesis Research|volume=142|issue=1|year=2019|pages=105–125|issn=0166-8595|doi=10.1007/s11120-019-00648-3|pmid=31187340|pmc=6763417|bibcode=2019PhoRe.142..105L }}</ref> using a variety of biophysical techniques. He has been recognized by a [[Festschrift]] for his contributions to [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) and its applications to chemical and biological systems.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/toc/jpcbfk/119/43|title=Wolfgang Lubitz Festschrift Special Issue|website=Journal of Physical Chemistry B Volume 119, Issue 43 (2015)|publisher=ACS Publications|access-date=December 5, 2019}}</ref>

== Education and career ==
He studied [[chemistry]] at the [[Free University Berlin]] from 1969 to 1974 and continued with his [[Dr. rer. nat.]] until 1977. From 1977 to 1982 he worked for his [[habilitation]] in [[organic chemistry]] at the Free University Berlin with a focus on [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR) and double resonance methods, such as [[ENDOR]]/TRIPLE. From 1979 to 1989 the FU Berlin employed him as an assistant professor, and as an associate professor at the Chemistry Department. From 1983 to 1984 he worked as a Max Kade Fellow at [[UC San Diego]] in the Physics Department with [[George Feher]] on EPR and ENDOR in [[photosynthesis]]. In 1989 he became an associate professor of experimental physics at the [[University of Stuttgart]]. In 1991 he returned to Berlin as a Full Professor and Chair of Physical Chemistry at the Max Volmer Institute at [[Technische Universität Berlin]]. He stayed until 2000 when he became a Scientific Member of the [[Max Planck Society]] and Director at the Max Planck Institute for Radiation Chemistry (in 2003 renamed Max Planck Institute for Bioinorganic Chemistry and in 2012 [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion]]) in [[Muelheim|Mülheim an der Ruhr]], [[North Rhine-Westphalia]], Germany. In the same year, he became honorary professor of the [[Heinrich-Heine-University]] of [[Düsseldorf]]. From 2004 to 2012, he was managing director of the [[Max Planck Institute]] and is currently a director ''emeritus'' of the [[Max Planck Institute for Chemical Energy Conversion]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cec.mpg.de/emeriti/|title=Wolfgang Lubitz (Emeriti)|website=Max Planck for Chemical Energy Conversion|publisher=Open Publishing|access-date=July 17, 2019}}</ref> Since 2004, he has been a member of the council for the [[Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings]], and has been its vice-president since 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lindau-nobel.org/wolfgang-lubitz/|title=Wolfgang Lubitz |website=The Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings|publisher=Open Publishing|access-date=July 17, 2019}}</ref>

== Research ==
His research focuses on the elementary processes of photosynthesis and catalytic metal centers in [[metalloproteins]]. He is an expert in the application of EPR spectroscopy and quantum chemical calculations. He has over 500 publications with more than 25,000 citations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.de/citations?hl=de&user=LDVyiJQAAAAJ|title=Wolfgang Lubitz (Google Scholar)|website=Google Scholar|publisher=Open Publishing|access-date=December 5, 2019}}</ref>

=== EPR spectroscopy ===
Throughout his career, EPR has played an important role as a biophysical technique to gain information about radicals, radical pairs, triplet states and metal centers in chemistry and biochemistry.<ref name="LubitzLendzian2002" /><ref name="LubitzReijerse2007">{{cite journal|last1=Lubitz|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Reijerse|first2=Eduard|last3=van Gastel|first3=Maurice|title=[NiFe] and [FeFe] Hydrogenases Studied by Advanced Magnetic Resonance Techniques|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=107|issue=10|year=2007|pages=4331–4365|issn=0009-2665|doi=10.1021/cr050186q|pmid=17845059}}</ref><ref name="CoxLubitz2013" /> Particular emphasis has been placed on methods that are able to resolve the electron-nuclear hyperfine couplings between the [[electron spin]] and the [[nuclear spin]]s. Next to the more established techniques, [[Pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance|electron spin echo modulation]] (ESEEM)  and [[ENDOR|electron-nuclear double resonance]] (ENDOR), his group further developed and used electron-electron double resonance- (ELDOR) detected [[Nuclear magnetic resonance|NMR]] (EDNMR) at a range of mw frequencies.<ref name="Cox2Lubitz2013">{{cite journal|last1=Cox|first1=N.|last2=Lubitz|first2=W.|last3=Savitsky|first3=A.|year=2013|title=W-band ELDOR-detected NMR (EDNMR) spectroscopy as a versatile technique for the characterisation of transition metal–ligand interactions|journal=Molecular Physics|volume=111|issue=18–19|pages=2788–2808|doi=10.1080/00268976.2013.830783|bibcode=2013MolPh.111.2788C|s2cid=97147588|issn=0026-8976}}</ref><ref name="NalepaMöbius2014">{{cite journal|last1=Nalepa|first1=A.|last2=Möbius|first2=K.|last3=Lubitz|first3=W.|last4=Savitsky|first4=A.|year=2014|title=High-field ELDOR-detected NMR study of a nitroxide radical in disordered solids: Towards characterization of heterogeneity of microenvironments in spin-labeled systems|journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance|volume=242|pages=203–213|doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2014.02.026|pmid=24685717|bibcode=2014JMagR.242..203N|issn=1090-7807}}</ref><ref name="CoxNalepa2015">{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=N.|title=Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Investigations of Biological Systems by Using Spin Labels, Spin Probes, and Intrinsic Metal Ions, Part A|last2=Nalepa|first2=A.|last3=Pandelia|first3=M.-E.|last4=Lubitz|first4=W.|last5=Savitsky|first5=A.|year=2015|chapter=Pulse Double-Resonance EPR Techniques for the Study of Metallobiomolecules|volume=563|pages=211–249|doi=10.1016/bs.mie.2015.08.016|issn=0076-6879|series=Methods in Enzymology|pmid=26478487|isbn=978-0-12-802834-6}}</ref> These techniques have been used by him and his group to extensively study bacterial [[photosynthetic reaction centre]]s, their donor-acceptor model complexes, [[photosystem I]], [[photosystem II]],<ref name="LubitzLendzian2002" /><ref name="CoxLubitz2013" /> and a number of different hydrogenases.<ref name="LubitzReijerse2007" /><ref name="LubitzHydrogenase2014" />

=== Oxygen-evolving Complex ===
During his early career, bacterial [[photosynthetic reaction centre]]s and oxygenic [[photosystem I]] and photosystem II<ref name="LubitzLendzian2002" /> have been a main focus. He and his group studied light-induced [[chlorophyll]] donor<ref name="LendzianHuber1993" /> and quinone acceptor radical ions<ref name="LubitzFeher1999" /> of the primary electron-transfer chain. Later his research focused on the [[Water oxidation catalysis|water splitting cycle]] (S-states) of [[photosystem II]] using advanced multifrequency pulse EPR, [[Electron nuclear double resonance|ENDOR]] and EDNMR techniques. His group was able to detect and characterize the flash-generated, freeze-trapped [[Paramagnetism|paramagnetic]] states S<sub>0</sub>, S<sub>2</sub> and S<sub>3</sub> (S<sub>1</sub> is diamagnetic and S<sub>4</sub> is a transient state) of the Mn<sub>4</sub>Ca<sub>1</sub>O<sub>x</sub> catalytic cluster. By a careful spectral analysis–backed up by [[Quantum chemistry|quantum chemical calculations]] the site [[oxidation]] and [[Spin states (d electrons)|spin states]] of all [[Manganese|Mn]] ions and their spin coupling for all intermediates of the [[catalytic cycle]] could be detected.<ref name="CoxRetegan2014">{{cite journal|last1=Cox|first1=N.|last2=Retegan|first2=M.|last3=Neese|first3=F.|last4=Pantazis|first4=D. A.|last5=Boussac|first5=A.|last6=Lubitz|first6=W.|title=Electronic structure of the oxygen-evolving complex in photosystem II prior to O-O bond formation|journal=Science|volume=345|issue=6198|year=2014|pages=804–808|issn=0036-8075|doi=10.1126/science.1254910|pmid=25124437|bibcode=2014Sci...345..804C|s2cid=13503746}}</ref><ref name="KrewaldRetegan2015">{{cite journal|last1=Krewald|first1=V.|last2=Retegan|first2=M.|last3=Cox|first3=N.|last4=Messinger|first4=J.|last5=Lubitz|first5=W.|last6=DeBeer|first6=S.|last7=Neese|first7=F.|last8=Pantazis|first8=D. A.|year=2015|title=Metal oxidation states in biological water splitting|journal=Chemical Science|volume=6|issue=3|pages=1676–1695|doi=10.1039/C4SC03720K|pmid=29308133|pmc=5639794|issn=2041-6520|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="KrewaldRetegan2016">{{cite journal|last1=Krewald|first1=V.|last2=Retegan|first2=M.|last3=Neese|first3=F.|last4=Lubitz|first4=W.|last5=Pantazis|first5=D. A.|last6=Cox|first6=N.|year=2016|title=Spin State as a Marker for the Structural Evolution of Nature's Water-Splitting Catalyst|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|volume=55|issue=2|pages=488–501|doi=10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5b02578|pmid=26700960|issn=0020-1669|hdl=1885/230998|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Further work using advanced Pulse EPR techniques, such as EDNMR, has led to information on the binding of water<ref name="RapatskiyCox2012">{{cite journal|last1=Rapatskiy|first1=Leonid|last2=Cox|first2=Nicholas|last3=Savitsky|first3=Anton|last4=Ames|first4=William M.|last5=Sander|first5=Julia|last6=Nowaczyk|first6=Marc. M.|last7=Rögner|first7=Matthias|last8=Boussac|first8=Alain|last9=Neese|first9=Frank|last10=Messinger|first10=Johannes|last11=Lubitz|first11=Wolfgang|title=Detection of the Water-Binding Sites of the Oxygen-Evolving Complex of Photosystem II Using W-Band 17O Electron–Electron Double Resonance-Detected NMR Spectroscopy|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=134|issue=40|year=2012|pages=16619–16634|issn=0002-7863|doi=10.1021/ja3053267|pmid=22937979|bibcode=2012JAChS.13416619R|url=https://zenodo.org/record/3424551}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> and a proposal of an efficient O-O bond formation in the final state of the cycle.<ref name="CoxRetegan2014" /><ref name="LubitzChrysina2019" />

=== [NiFe]- and [FeFe]-hydrogenase ===
Extensive work was performed on the [[NiFe hydrogenase|[NiFe]-Hydrogenase]] where the magnetic tensors were measured and related to quantum chemical calculations.<ref name="LubitzReijerse2007" /><ref name="LubitzHydrogenase2014" /> Through his work, the structures of all intermediates in the activation path and catalytic cycle of [NiFe]-hydrogenases were obtained. In the course of this work a 0.89 [[Ångström]] resolution [[X-ray crystallography|X-ray crystallography diffraction]] model of [NiFe]-hydrogenase was achieved.<ref name="OgataNishikawa2015">{{cite journal|last1=Ogata|first1=H.|last2=Nishikawa|first2=K.|last3=Lubitz|first3=W.|year=2015|title=Hydrogens detected by subatomic resolution protein crystallography in a [NiFe] hydrogenase|journal=Nature|volume=520|issue=7548|pages=571–574|doi=10.1038/nature14110|pmid=25624102|bibcode=2015Natur.520..571O|s2cid=4464257|issn=0028-0836}}</ref>

Similar work has been accomplished for the [FeFe]-hydrogenases.<ref name="LubitzHydrogenase2014" /> A key contribution of his research was the EPR spectroscopic evidence of an azapropane-dithiolate-ligand (ADT-ligand) in the dithiol bridge of the [FeFe]-hydrogenase active site <ref name="SilakovWenk2009">{{cite journal|last1=Silakov|first1=A.|last2=Wenk|first2=B.|last3=Reijerse|first3=E.J.|last4=Lubitz|first4=W.|year=2009|title=<sup>14</sup>N HYSCORE investigation of the H-cluster of [FeFe] hydrogenase: evidence for a nitrogen in the dithiol bridge|journal=Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics|volume=11|issue=31|pages=6592–9|doi=10.1039/b905841a|pmid=19639134|bibcode=2009PCCP...11.6592S|issn=1463-9076}}</ref> and the determination of the magnitude and orientation of the g-tensor using single crystal EPR.<ref name="SidabrasDuan2019">{{cite journal|last1=Sidabras|first1=Jason W.|last2=Duan|first2=Jifu|last3=Winkler|first3=Martin|last4=Happe|first4=Thomas|last5=Hussein|first5=Rana|last6=Zouni|first6=Athina|last7=Suter|first7=Dieter|last8=Schnegg|first8=Alexander|last9=Lubitz|first9=Wolfgang|last10=Reijerse|first10=Edward J.|title=Extending electron paramagnetic resonance to nanoliter volume protein single crystals using a self-resonant microhelix|journal=Science Advances|volume=5|issue=10|year=2019|article-number=eaay1394|issn=2375-2548|doi=10.1126/sciadv.aay1394|pmid=31620561|pmc=6777973|bibcode=2019SciA....5.1394S|doi-access=free}}</ref> The ADT-ligand was later confirmed by artificial maturation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases.<ref name="BerggrenAdamska2013">{{cite journal|last1=Berggren|first1=G.|last2=Adamska|first2=A.|last3=Lambertz|first3=C.|last4=Simmons|first4=T. R.|last5=Esselborn|first5=J.|last6=Atta|first6=M.|last7=Gambarelli|first7=S.|last8=Mouesca|first8=J.-M.|last9=Reijerse|first9=E.|year=2013|title=Biomimetic assembly and activation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases|journal=Nature|volume=499|issue=7456|pages=66–69|doi=10.1038/nature12239|pmid=23803769|issn=0028-0836|last10=Lubitz|first10=W.|last11=Happe|first11=T.|last12=Artero|first12=V.|last13=Fontecave|first13=M.|pmc=3793303|bibcode=2013Natur.499...66B}}</ref> Using artificial maturation, the protein could be generated without the co-factor ([[Enzyme#Cofactors|apoprotein]]) using E. coli [[mutagenesis]] and a synthetically created active site could be inserted,<ref name="BerggrenAdamska2013" /><ref name="EsselbornLambertz2013">{{cite journal|last1=Esselborn|first1=J.|last2=Lambertz|first2=C.|last3=Adamska-Venkatesh|first3=A.|last4=Simmons|first4=T.|last5=Berggren|first5=G.|last6=Noth|first6=J.|last7=Siebel|first7=J.|last8=Hemschemeier|first8=A.|last9=Artero|first9=V.|year=2013|title=Spontaneous activation of [FeFe]-hydrogenases by an inorganic [2Fe] active site mimic|journal=Nature Chemical Biology|volume=9|issue=10|pages=607–609|doi=10.1038/nchembio.1311|pmid=23934246|issn=1552-4450|last10=Reijerse|first10=E. J.|last11=Fontecave|first11=M.|last12=Lubitz|first12=W.|last13=Happe|first13=T.|pmc=3795299}}</ref><ref name="SiebelAdamska-Venkatesh2015">{{cite journal|last1=Siebel|first1=Judith F.|last2=Adamska-Venkatesh|first2=Agnieszka|last3=Weber|first3=Katharina|last4=Rumpel|first4=Sigrun|last5=Reijerse|first5=Edward|last6=Lubitz|first6=Wolfgang|title=Hybrid [FeFe]-Hydrogenases with Modified Active Sites Show Remarkable Residual Enzymatic Activity|journal=Biochemistry|volume=54|issue=7|year=2015|pages=1474–1483|issn=0006-2960|doi=10.1021/bi501391d|pmid=25633077}}</ref> which has opened new vistas in hydrogenase research.<ref name="BirrellRüdiger2017">{{cite journal|last1=Birrell|first1=James A.|last2=Rüdiger|first2=Olaf|last3=Reijerse|first3=Edward J.|last4=Lubitz|first4=Wolfgang|title=Semisynthetic Hydrogenases Propel Biological Energy Research into a New Era|journal=Joule|volume=1|issue=1|year=2017|pages=61–76|issn=2542-4351|doi=10.1016/j.joule.2017.07.009|doi-access=free|bibcode=2017Joule...1...61B }}</ref>

== Awards and recognition ==

* Otto-Klung-Preis für Chemie, FU Berlin (1978)
* Max-Kade-Fellowship, New York (1983)
* International Zavoisky Award, Russian and Tatarstan Academy of Sciences, Kazan, Russia (2002)
* Bruker Prize, Royal Society of Chemistry, ESR group, U.K. (2003)
* Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry. U.K. (2004)
* Gold Medal of the International EPR Society (2005)
* Honorary doctorate Dr. h. c., Uppsala University, Sweden (2008) 
* Fellow of ISMAR (International Society of Magnetic Resonance)  (2010)
* Foreign Member of the Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Tatarstan (2012)
* Honorary doctorate, Dr. h.c., Université d'Aix-Marseille, France (2014) 
* Robert Bunsen Vorlesung, Deutsche Bunsen-Gesellschaft für Physikalische Chemie e.V. (2017)
* Fellow of the International EPR Society (2017)
